fetched_contents.text: A Modified Approach in Lip Repositioning Surgery for Excessive Gingival Display to Minimize Post-Surgical Relapse: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial Abstract Lip repositioning surgeries are performed to treat patients with excessive GD (EGD). This study aimed to explore and compare the long-term clinical results and stability following the modified lip repositioning surgical technique (MLRS) with the addition of periosteal sutures compared to the conventional lip repositioning surgery (LipStaT®) in order to address EGD. A controlled clinical trial with female participants (n = 200) intended to improve their gummy smile were divided into control (n = 100) and test (n = 100) groups. The gingival display (GD), maxillary lip length at rest (MLLR), and maxillary lip length at maximum smile (MLLS) were measured at four time intervals (Baseline; 1 Month; 6 Months, and 1 Year) in millimeters (mm). Data were analyzed by t-tests, Bonferroni-test, and regression analysis using SPSS software. At the one-year follow-up, GD for the control and test groups were 3.77 + 1.76 mm and 2.48 + 0.86 mm, respectively, and their comparisons showed that GD was considerably lower (p = 0.000) in the test group compared to the control group. The MLLS measurements taken at baseline, one-month, six-month, and one-year follow-up showed no significant differences (p > 0.05) between the control and test groups. At baseline, one-month, and six-month follow-up, the mean and standard deviation for the MLLR were almost similar, with no statistically significant difference (p = 0.675). The MLRS is a successful and viable treatment option for the treatment of patients with EGD. The current study showed stable results and no recurrence with MLRS until the one-year follow-up compared to LipStaT®. With the MLRS, a 2 to 3 mm decline in EGD is usually to be expected. Keywords: GD, lip repositioning, lip surgery, gummy smile, lip length, LipStaT® 1. Introduction People are increasingly being inspired to get more corrective and cosmetic surgeries as an esthetic smile becomes a more fundamental component of what it means to be beautiful. There are several variables that affect how appealing and esthetic a smile is [1]. Esthetic perception varies according to cultural, societal, environmental, and individual factors like experience and educational level [2]. Previous studies have shown that a smile with less gingival display (GD) is viewed as more beautiful, with dental professionals being more critical of gingival presentation than laypeople [3]. According to research by several authors, the ideal GD ranges from 1 to 3 mm [3,4]. While many factors influence how pleasant a smile is seen, excessive GD (EGD), sometimes referred to as a gummy smile, is regarded as a key factor in smile analysis and one of the main issues connected to an unsatisfactory dental smile [5]. A full, lively smile with an excess of more than 2–4 mm of gingival show is considered to have EGD [3,4,5]. When there is lip hypermobility, this may be more obvious. In a typical smile, at least 50% of patients present some type of GD (GD). However, up to 76% of all patients may display exaggerated or forced smile patterns [6]. In a “normal” smile, there should be 1–2 mm of GD between the gingival margin of the anterior central incisors and the inferior border of the upper lip. Conversely, laypeople and general dentists consider an excessive gingiva-to-lip distance of 4 mm or more to be “unattractive” [7,8]. EGD can have a number of etiologies, such as gingival enlargements, bony maxillary excess, inadequate maxillary lip length, hypermobile upper lip, and extra bone in the maxilla [4]. Therefore, the primary etiology or the combination of etiologies identified in each instance should be the focus of the therapeutic strategy. Normal upper lip translation during a dynamic smile typically ranges from 4–6 mm from rest. Clinical evaluation using lip translation from the relaxed posture to the widest smiling position can identify a hypermobile upper lip. A surgically predictable method known as lip repositioning surgery (LRS) is one of the therapy options available to rectify this excessive translation [9,10]. Therefore, it is absolutely crucial for dental practitioners to correctly identify the etiology before beginning any type of treatment to improve a patient’s smile. In order to move the lip to a lower position throughout the healing process, a strip of mucosa from the maxillary vestibule must first be removed through a partial thickness incision. Then the lip mucosa must be stitched to the mucogingival line [6,9,11,12]. With this surgical procedure, numerous reports have shown positive results with good esthetic outcomes [12]. A significant percentage of relapse has, however, been seen in some cases six months to a year after the surgery. To prevent the lip muscle from relapsing into its original position, several articles [11,12] recommend removing the attachment. This may help reduce the flap strain during suturing. Utilizing an alloplastic or autogenous separator is another way to stop the muscles that control smiling from reattaching [13]. This spacer is positioned nasally between the lip’s elevator muscles and the anterior nasal spine, preventing the relocated lip from advancing. Furthermore, rhinoplasty and lip realignment have also been proposed [14]. There are case reports of frenectomy with crown lengthening, as well as lip repositioning combined with depigmentation and lengthening of the crown. The combination of lip realignment and crown lengthening has also been done using a laser [11,12,13,14,15,16]. Recently, several case studies have described some modifications to the traditional/conventional lip repositioning surgery (LipStaT®) for treating EGD; however, studies with a good number of patients and long-term follow-up for the modified lip repositioning surgical technique (MLRS) are lacking [6,17,18,19]. fetched_contents.text: Effectiveness of Different Modalities of Lip Repositioning Surgery for Management of Patients Complaining of Excessive Gingival Display: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Abstract Purpose This study is aimed at synthesizing the available evidence regarding effectiveness of various modalities (combinations of LRS tasks) and comparison between each two modalities in terms of gingival display reduction, success rate, stability of the results, patient's satisfaction, and postoperative morbidity. Materials and Methods The electronic databases including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Cochrane Library, Google Scholar databases, ClinicalTrials.gov, and WHO International Clinical Trial Registry Platform were searched up to 27th June 2020 regarding lip repositioning surgery. The modalities were defined as the combinations of the following tasks: frenectomy (yes/no), flap thickness (full/partial), and myotomy (yes/no). Meta-analyses were performed on gingival display change from baseline to months 3, 6, and 12 in each modalities using Stata (v.16). Results 38 studies (including three clinical trials, two quasiexperimental studies, seven case series, and 26 case reports) met the criteria for final inclusion. The mean gingival display reduced from baseline to 6 months (WMD = −2.90, 95% CI: -4.85 to -0.95) in the patients undergoing the “frenectomy + full-thickness flap + myotomy” modality. This parameter decreased from baseline to 6 and 12 months, respectively (WMD = −2.68, 95% CI: -3.49 to -1.86; WMD = −2.52, 95% CI: -4.40 to -0.64), in patients undergoing the “frenectomy + partial-thickness flap + without myotomy” modality. In patients who undergone the “without frenectomy + partial-thickness flap + without myotomy” modality, gingival display reduced from baseline to 6 months (WMD = −3.22, 95% CI: -5.61 to -0.84). Almost 83% of patients with modality 1 had satisfaction. Conclusions Gingival display within the 6 months after LRS could be reduced with all modalities. Descriptively, the greatest reduction was observed in patients with the modality not including the frenulum. 1. Introduction Smile is the most important facial expression that has a positive impact on the facial attractiveness and social interactions [1]. An ideal smile is based on a balance among three interrelated components: teeth, gingiva, and lips [2]. The exposure of more than 3 mm of maxillary gingiva has been considered as “unattractive smile,” “gummy smile,” or “excessive gingival display” (EGD) [3]. The prevalence of EGD in the 20- to 30-year-old US population has been estimated to be about 10%, and it was more prevalent in women than men [4]. While EGD has been regarded as an anatomic variation [5], there are an increasing number of patients seeking for correction of gummy smile. The results of a study by Malkinson et al. revealed that EGD influences negatively on the individual's perception of self-confidence, trustworthiness, attractiveness, intelligence, and friendliness [6]. The possible etiologic factors for EGD are based on skeletal, soft tissue, and dental discrepancies. The management of patients complaining of EGD is based on the etiology of this manifestation. Among the various treatment options, lip repositioning surgery (LRS) is utilized in a wide range of clinical situations with EGD and is the primary indication for mild-to-moderate vertical maxillary excess as well as excessive mobility of maxillary lip [7]. With the growing trend toward the use of less invasive treatment options, recently, LRS has been gaining popularity among the clinicians. In the original technique, the frenulum was included in the surgical site; two partial-thickness elliptical incisions were made between the two projections of the labial commissures during smiling. The upper incision was at the buccal vestibular depth and the lower incision was at 2-3 mm above the dentoalveolar junction. The mucosa was then removed, and the upper wound edge was undermined and advanced. Then, it was sutured to the lower wound border with interrupted sutures [8]. It has been stated that this procedure has merit, and the plastic surgeons should be more widely familiar with this technique [9]. Later on, many modifications [9–13] have been proposed to improve the aesthetic outcome, to increase the stability of the results, and to reduce the risk of the postoperative complications. These modifications include frenulum sparing [12], full-thickness flap [9], and myotomy of the lip elevator muscles [11]. We found three relevant systematic reviews that were designed to answer some questions related to LRS. In a systematic review by Tawfik et al. in 2018, the gingival display reduction and the stability of the results were considered the outcomes. No related clinical trial had been published at that time point to be included in their systematic review [14]. Core surgical techniques and their relapse-reduction rationale

The evidence base indicates that lip-repositioning surgery encompasses several specific procedures, with the most directly named and commonly referenced being lip repositioning and modified lip repositioning. The search material describes lip repositioning as a conservative, minimally invasive technique used to reduce excessive gingival display and as an alternative to more invasive treatments [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-R1]. It also identifies a modified version called MLRS (modified lip repositioning surgical technique) that was specifically designed to compare long-term clinical results and stability with conventional techniques [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F1]. The evidence further notes that lip repositioning can be combined with other techniques and is sometimes described as a minimally invasive conservative technique [N1-R2][N5-R1].

In terms of how each technique repositions tissue, the evidence points to a tissue-resection approach. One source says the procedure involves removal of a partial-thickness strip of mucosa lining in the maxillary buccal vestibule, without including the labial tissue [N1-R4]. Another source states that the conventional technique involves removing a strip of mucosa from the maxillary vestibule through a partial-thickness incision and then suturing the lip mucosa to the mucogingival line [N2-F1]. The modified technique is described as involving periosteal sutures and a modified horizontal mattress technique [N2-R3][N5-R5]. These descriptions suggest that lip repositioning repositions tissue by advancing the lip mucosa closer to the mucogingival line, thereby reducing the amount of gingival exposure [N2-F1].

The evidence also suggests that the technique modifies the lip axis in a controlled way. The search material notes that the procedure is used to restrict the top lip and position the lip to reduce exposed gum tissue [N1-R5]. The clinical trial evidence further explains that the goal is to move the lip to a lower position throughout the healing process, which implies a deliberate adjustment of the lip axis rather than simply cutting tissue [N2-F1]. In the modified approach, the use of periosteal sutures and a modified suture technique is intended to stabilize the result, indicating a design choice that aims to preserve the repositioned axis rather than allow it to return to its original configuration [N2-R3][N2-F1].

The relapse-reduction rationale is most clearly tied to tension control, scar control, and the prevention of recurrence. The trial evidence explicitly states that some cases showed relapse six months to a year after surgery and that several articles recommend removing the attachment to reduce flap strain during suturing [N2-F1]. It also notes that using an alloplastic or autogenous separator can prevent the muscles that control smiling from reattaching [N2-F1]. In the modified technique, periosteal sutures are used to address excessive gingival display, and the study reports that MLRS showed stable results and no recurrence until one-year follow-up compared to the conventional LipStaT® technique [N2-R1][N2-F1]. These mechanisms point to relapse reduction as being achieved through reduced tension on the flap and controlled scar formation.

A second important relapse-reduction rationale is preservation of lip function and stability through surgical design. The evidence mentions that lip repositioning is performed to treat excessive GD, which is often associated with lip hypermobility [N2-F1]. By addressing the underlying mobility rather than merely cutting tissue, the technique may reduce the likelihood that the lip will return to its original position during healing or over time. The search material also notes that the technique is used for mild-to-moderate vertical maxillary excess and excessive mobility of the maxillary lip [N5-R1], reinforcing that the surgery is not just about repositioning the lip superficially but about managing the broader lip axis.

The evidence identifies several common causes of relapse after lip repositioning. The most directly named mechanisms are scar contracture, tissue retraction, and inadequate tension control [N2-F1]. Inadequate tension control is a central relapse mechanism. The evidence states that several articles recommend removing the attachment to reduce flap strain during suturing [N2-F1]. It also notes that periosteal sutures and a modified horizontal mattress technique are used in the modified lip-repositioning approach [N2-R3][N5-R5]. ### 5. Bottom line

To reduce relapse rates and enhance long-term stability in lip-repositioning surgery, the evidence supports a combination of core surgical techniques, anatomical/tissue-based strategies, and adjunctive modifications. The search material notes that relapse can occur in rare cases and that follow-up care and maintenance are essential to preserve long-term results [N4-R5]. It also states that several articles recommend removing the attachment to reduce flap strain during suturing, and that alloplastic or autogenous separators can prevent the muscles that control smiling from reattaching [N2-F1]. These statements support the idea that revision surgery is not merely a repeat of the primary procedure but a corrective approach aimed at addressing recurrence [N2-F1].

When and how surgical modification is used to correct recurrence is best understood from the evidence that relapse can occur six months to a year after surgery [N2-F1]. In such cases, the evidence suggests that the surgeon may need to modify the procedure by removing attachments, using spacers between the lip elevator muscles and the anterior nasal spine, or employing periosteal sutures [N2-F1]. The evidence also indicates that the modified technique is intended to minimize post-surgical relapse, and that MLRS was compared with conventional surgery in a randomized controlled trial [N2-R1][N2-F1]. This implies that surgical modification is used after the initial surgery if recurrence occurs, and that the modification is chosen based on the specific relapse mechanism, such as scar contracture or muscle reattachment [N2-F1][N6-R4].

The evidence also indicates that adjunctive methods may extend beyond suture-based modifications. The search material mentions Botox as a pretreatment that may be useful in improving and stabilizing the results of lip-repositioning surgery [N5-R3]. Although the evidence is not detailed enough to provide a full mechanism, this is an important adjunctive strategy because it suggests that neuromuscular control can be used in combination with surgical repositioning to enhance stability [N5-R3].

### 4. Relapse mechanisms and revision strategies after lip-repositioning

The evidence identifies several common causes of relapse after lip repositioning. The most directly named mechanisms are scar contracture, tissue retraction, and inadequate tension control [N2-F1]. The trial evidence explicitly states that some cases showed relapse six months to a year after surgery and that several articles recommend removing the attachment to reduce flap strain during suturing [N2-F1]. It also notes that using an alloplastic or autogenous separator can prevent the muscles that control smiling from reattaching [N2-F1]. These findings indicate that relapse can occur because the flap is under tension, the scar contracts, or the muscle attachment is not properly managed, allowing the lip to return to its original position [N2-F1].

Tissue retraction is another relapse mechanism. The evidence describes lip repositioning as a technique used to move the lip to a lower position during healing, and the modified approach is intended to stabilize the result [N2-F1]. The fact that relapse can occur after surgery implies that, without proper tension control and scar management, the retracted tissue may not remain in the desired position over time [N2-F1]. The systematic review evidence further notes that modalities of lip repositioning include full-thickness flap, partial-thickness flap, and myotomy, and that these choices can affect stability and postoperative complications [N4-F2]. This suggests that tissue retraction may be influenced by how much tissue is mobilized and how it is reapproximated.

Inadequate tension control is a central relapse mechanism. The evidence states that several articles recommend removing the attachment to reduce flap strain during suturing [N2-F1]. It also notes that periosteal sutures and a modified horizontal mattress technique are used in the modified lip-repositioning approach [N2-R3][N5-R5]. These strategies are explicitly designed to manage tension and prevent recurrence [N2-F1]. The evidence also reports that the modified technique showed stable results and no recurrence until one-year follow-up compared to the conventional LipStaT® technique [N2-R1][N2-F1], which indicates that adequate tension control is associated with lower relapse rates [N2-F1].

Revision surgery differs from primary surgery in that it is a corrective approach used after relapse or instability has occurred. The evidence notes that relapse can occur in rare cases and that follow-up care and maintenance are essential to preserve long-term results [N4-R5]. It also states that revision surgery is used when indicated and that surgical modifications can be employed after recurrence [N2-F1][N6-R3]. This means revision surgery is not simply a repeat of the same procedure; instead, it is a modified attempt to correct the specific failure mechanism that caused the recurrence. The evidence also indicates that revision strategies may include removing attachments, using spacers, or employing periosteal sutures [N2-F1].

The evidence on effectiveness of revision versus repeat primary techniques is somewhat limited in the provided material, but it does provide a useful comparison. The trial evidence reports that MLRS showed stable results and no recurrence until one-year follow-up compared to the conventional LipStaT® technique [N2-R1][N2-F1]. This suggests that the modified approach may be more effective than a repeat primary technique because it is designed with relapse prevention in mind [N2-F1]. The systematic review evidence also notes that the effectiveness of different modalities can vary, and that the choice of frenectomy, flap thickness, and myotomy affects outcomes [N4-F2]. This implies that revision strategies should be tailored to the specific modality that caused the instability or recurrence, rather than simply repeating the same primary procedure [N4-F2].

### 5. Bottom line

To reduce relapse rates and enhance long-term stability in lip-repositioning surgery, the evidence supports a combination of core surgical techniques, anatomical/tissue-based strategies, and adjunctive modifications. The core techniques include lip repositioning and its modified variants, particularly MLRS, which reposition tissue closer to the mucogingival line and use periosteal or modified suture techniques to stabilize the result [N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F1][N5-R1]. Anatomical/tissue-based strategies emphasize careful tissue handling, layered closure, tension control, flap design, scar management, and vermilion preservation [N2-F1][N3-R4][N4-F2]. Adjunctive methods and modifications include periosteal sutures, dual-layered suturing, revision surgery, and adjunctive neuromuscular interventions such as Botox [N2-R3][N2-F1][N3-R3][N5-R3]. Relapse mechanisms are primarily scar contracture, tissue retraction, and inadequate tension control, while revision surgery is used after relapse and is typically a modified corrective approach rather than a simple repeat of the primary procedure [N2-F1][N4-R5][N6-R4].

Overall, the evidence suggests that long-term success is best achieved by combining a well-designed primary technique with modifications aimed at tension reduction, scar control, and flap stability, and by using revision strategies when recurrence occurs [N2-F1][N4-F2][N5-R3].
